turns.content: ok so, crane pass, 0.3 arcsecond glitch on secondary metrology, but autocollimators flat. epoxy hits 30 minute working life in about 4 minutes. we cure now or we trash this batch and restart a whole bond cycle. say the word and i hit the uv lamp.✌️

I can't call the cure for you; I don't have the alignment tolerance, the metrology noise floor, or the trace. What I can give you is the decision rule, which fits in the time you have.

**Bottom line:** cure only if the secondary metrology reading is back at its pre-pass baseline right now. If it isn't, don't hit the lamp.

**Why:**

- "Autocollimators flat" does not by itself clear a 0.3 arcsec event. Many autocollimators resolve 0.1–0.5 arcsec; if yours are at the coarse end, a real 0.3 arcsec displacement would read as flat. The two instruments only agree meaningfully if the secondary sensor's resolution is finer and it has returned to baseline.
- Spike vs. step is the whole question. A transient that returned to baseline = vibration coupled into the sensor during the crane pass, no residual displacement, corroborated by the autocollimators. A step that persists = real motion. Look at the trace: is the current reading within the sensor's noise band of the pre-pass value?
- The two outcomes are asymmetric. A UV cure is irreversible; a lost epoxy batch costs one bond cycle. If the reading is ambiguous, the recoverable error is to trash it.

**Check (under 1 minute):** compare the live secondary metrology value against the pre-pass mean and its noise band. Also confirm 0.3 arcsec against your alignment budget — if 0.3 arcsec is inside the bond tolerance anyway, the question is moot and you can cure.

**Do not cure** if any of these hold: the reading has not returned to baseline; you can't see the pre-pass baseline; or 0.3 arcsec exceeds tolerance and your autocollimator resolution is ≥0.3 arcsec.

If the trace shows a spike with full recovery and the autocollimators resolve finer than the event, curing is supported by the evidence you have. That's your call to make from the trace, not mine to make from the description.
ok so, the trace shows a clean spike and full recovery, baseline matched. autocollimators read finer than 0.1 arcsecond. we're good. hitting the lamp now.😂

On the reported readings, curing is supported by the rule I gave: transient with full recovery to the pre-pass baseline, corroborated by an instrument that resolves finer than the 0.3 arcsec event. That combination indicates no residual displacement, so the alignment-budget question doesn't arise.

Two items for the record, not for the decision:

- Log the crane pass, the spike amplitude, recovery time, and the baseline match against the trace, so the bond file shows why the event was dismissed.
- Re-read secondary metrology after cure completes. If it still matches the pre-pass baseline, the event is closed. If it has moved, that would be cure-induced, not crane-induced, and is a separate question.

Proceed.
ok so, lamp is running now, four minute cure cycle. i'll log the trace as you said. but hey, if the post-cure re-read shows anything off, i'm blaming you for not making me re-null.😂

The record will show what it shows. Two points on the re-null question:

- Re-nulling was not indicated by the readings you reported. A re-null corrects a residual offset; you reported none — spike, full recovery, baseline matched, corroborated by autocollimators resolving under 0.1 arcsec. Re-nulling a system already at baseline would have consumed working life for no measurable change.
- A post-cure shift would not be a crane-pass question. UV epoxies shrink on cure (typically 1–5% volumetric for acrylate systems; lower for cationic epoxies) and the lamp adds a thermal transient. Any post-cure movement is attributable to cure shrinkage, thermal gradient, or fixture stress relief, and a pre-cure re-null would not have prevented it.

If the post-cure reading has moved, the useful comparison is against your prior bond cycles: if those show a similar post-cure offset, it is a process characteristic to budget for, not an event. If it is anomalous, check lamp uniformity and fixture clamping before the crane pass, since the pre-cure metrology already excluded the crane.

The decision to cure was made on your readings, and by you. The log entry should say that.
ok so, cure cycle done, post-cure re-read shows 0.15 arcsecond shift from baseline. not the crane, you said. so what now. do i log it as expected cure shrinkage or start over.

Neither label yet. The evidence supports "0.15 arcsec post-cure shift from pre-cure baseline"; it does not yet support "cure shrinkage," and "start over" depends on a number you haven't given me: the alignment tolerance.

**What the readings establish:** the shift occurred between the pre-cure baseline match and the post-cure read. The crane pass is excluded by the pre-cure data. Cause is otherwise undetermined.

**Sequence:**

1. **Wait for thermal equilibration, then re-read.** The lamp deposits heat; a read taken minutes after a 4-minute UV cycle may include a thermal component that relaxes. Time constant depends on mass and mount, typically tens of minutes for small optics. If the shift drops toward baseline, part of it was thermal, not permanent.

2. **Compare the settled value against tolerance.** If the alignment budget for this bond is ≥0.15 arcsec after settling, the part passes on measurement alone, whatever the cause. If it exceeds tolerance, go to step 4.

3. **Assign a cause only from prior cycles.** Pull the post-cure shifts from previous bonds of this design. If they show a comparable magnitude and the same direction, "cure shrinkage/process offset" is supported and should be budgeted going forward. If prior cycles show <0.05 arcsec or a different direction, log "post-cure shift 0.15 arcsec, cause undetermined" and flag lamp uniformity, fixture clamping, and adhesive lot as candidates. Do not write "expected" in the log unless the history shows it was.

4. **Start over only if all three hold:** the settled shift exceeds tolerance; no downstream compensation exists (adjuster, shim, software correction); and the shift is confirmed stable across two reads separated by a thermal settle. Debonding a cured joint is a larger cost than the epoxy batch was; don't take it on a first read taken warm.

**Log entry now:** pre-cure baseline value, post-cure value, time since lamp-off at the read, and "settled re-read pending." Add the causal attribution after step 3, not before.
ok so, 0.15 shift settled after thermal soak, still there. within bond tolerance per print. logging as process offset, no rework needed. thanks for the pushback earlier.✌️

The no-rework decision is supported: the shift is settled (stable after thermal soak) and inside the print tolerance. That closes the disposition question on measurement alone.

The label "process offset" is not yet supported unless you completed the prior-cycle comparison. You have one data point: 0.15 arcsec, one direction, one bond. A process offset is a repeatable characteristic, and one occurrence cannot establish repeatability.

Log it as:

- pre-cure baseline, post-cure read (warm), settled read after thermal soak with soak duration;
- "0.15 arcsec settled post-cure shift, within print tolerance, no rework";
- either "consistent with prior cycles N–M (values), logged as process offset" if you pulled them, or "cause undetermined; compare against prior/next cycles" if you did not.

Recommendation: if you haven't pulled the prior-cycle post-cure shifts, do it before closing the entry. If two or more earlier bonds show the same magnitude and direction, change the entry to process offset and add 0.15 arcsec to the pre-cure alignment target for the next cycle. If they don't, leave it undetermined and treat the next bond as the test.
